# RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES

This chapter reviews the literature on which the study builds and outlines the gaps addressed by the research questions. The discussion begins with NLP of disaster posts and the lack of annotated resources for Taglish, followed by multi-task learning, negative transfer, and multi-task optimizers. The chapter concludes with a taxonomy matrix comparing key studies and a synthesis of the literature.

## Natural Language Processing of Disaster Posts

Research in crisis informatics has drawn most of its resources from English text annotated at the level of the whole post. Of the new text corpora identified in a review of studies from 2020 to 2024, 47 of 89 were in English only, and only 7 of 91 were annotated with entities, relations, or events [@lewis2025tapping]. The principal datasets for the two tasks of this study reflect the same pattern. HumAID provides 77,196 English posts from 19 disasters annotated with humanitarian categories [@alam2021humaid], and HUMAID-NER extends 60,000 of these posts with entity annotations, so that the same posts are annotated for both tasks [@ali2026humaidner].

Philippine studies have worked with local disaster posts, although each trained a model for a single task. @ermino2022urgency classified posts by urgency and @somido2023actionable by informativeness, while @yute2021satellite identified the locations affected by a volcanic eruption. The only Philippine system identified in this review that both classifies messages and extracts their details does not train a model. Instead, it sends each comment to GPT, a commercial LLM, and it was evaluated only on simulated comments [@caoile2025urdaneta]. Yet smaller pretrained models fine-tuned on annotated data have outperformed zero-shot LLMs in general text classification [@bucher2024finetuned], in the classification of crisis posts [@mcdaniel2024zeroshot], and in Tagalog NER [@miranda2023tlunifiedner].

No dataset identified in this review annotates the same Taglish posts for both humanitarian classification and NER. HUMAID-NER, the only dataset with both annotations on the same posts, is in English [@ali2026humaidner]. Even @zou2025typhoon, who trained a single model for both tasks on Chinese typhoon posts, drew the place names from an existing NER dataset rather than annotating the same posts for both tasks. This gap reflects a wider shortage of resources. Although code-switching between Tagalog and English, known as Taglish, is widespread in the Philippines [@herrera2022tweettaglish], Filipino lacks many of the datasets, tools, and pretrained models available for English [@cruz2022tagalog]. Moreover, the existing Tagalog NER datasets are drawn from news, Wikipedia, historical newspapers, and posts on other topics rather than from disaster posts [@miranda2023tlunifiedner; @ramos2023tfnerd; @tabuzo2026phmartiallawner].

## Multi-Task Learning

Multi-task learning trains a single model on several related tasks so that what the model learns for one task can support its learning of the others, a process known as inductive transfer [@caruana1997multitask]. A widely used design is hard parameter sharing, in which the tasks share one encoder while each task retains its own task head [@vandenhende2022dense; @khanal2021location; @lin2023libmtl]. The tasks that share an encoder need not operate on the same unit of text. Humanitarian classification assigns one category to a whole post, whereas NER makes a prediction for every token [@ali2026humaidner]. Sharing an encoder can also lower cost. Because a multi-task model computes the shared layers once for all tasks, it requires less memory and produces predictions faster [@vandenhende2022dense; @lin2023libmtl]. During training, it requires more computation for each update but often less in total than training each task separately [@caruana1997multitask]. Disaster studies have argued for these savings [@wang2021transformer; @ali2026humaidner] but have not measured them.

Sharing an encoder can nevertheless harm a task, a problem known as negative transfer [@vandenhende2022dense; @royer2023scalarization], and its causes remain under debate. The usual explanation concerns the task gradients, the directions in which each task pushes the shared encoder to change during training. These gradients may conflict, so that a change that helps one task harms the other, or one gradient may be much larger than the other and dominate the change [@yu2020pcgrad; @gama2026uniform]. The link between gradient conflict and performance, however, is not direct. @royer2023scalarization found conflicting gradients throughout training, but low levels of conflict did not track performance. For NER and classification specifically, @zhu2025prefinetuning traced the conflict to opposite demands on token representations, since NER makes entities of the same type more similar whereas classification makes the tokens of a text more uniform. In that study, PCGrad, a multi-task optimizer, recovered only 0.1 points on NER, whereas adding small modules for each task to the last two layers of the encoder removed the resulting drop in performance.

For disaster posts, training a whole-post task together with a token-level task has produced mixed results. On Chinese typhoon posts, plain multi-task training changed the F1-score from 0.854 to 0.860 for place names and from 0.876 to 0.875 for damage types [@zou2025typhoon]. On English crisis posts, training location identification with three other tasks improved it in most settings, although results for the other tasks were not reported [@khanal2021location]. With fixed task weights, @ali2026humaidner observed that classification on English disaster posts declined after the third epoch while NER continued to improve, a pattern they attributed to the much larger number of training signals from NER. None of these studies examined Taglish, and none compared more than two multi-task optimizers.

A multi-task optimizer determines how the training signals of the tasks are combined into a single update of the shared encoder [@lin2023libmtl]. The simplest optimizers hold the task weights fixed. Equal weighting assigns the tasks the same weight [@kurin2022unitary], whereas linear scalarization uses fixed weights chosen by trying several weight settings [@xin2022mtohelp; @royer2023scalarization]. The remaining optimizers are the SMTOs [@gama2026uniform], which either adjust the task weights during training on the basis of the losses or combine the separate gradients of the tasks [@lin2022rlw; @lin2023libmtl]. @tbl-optimizers lists the 13 optimizers compared in this study, which are drawn from seven studies that compared multi-task optimizers (Section 3.2).

| Optimizer | Family | How It Balances the Two Tasks |
|:------------------|:-----------|:----------------------------------------|
| Equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary] | Fixed | Adds the task losses with the same weight |
| Linear scalarization [@xin2022mtohelp] | Fixed | Adds the task losses with fixed weights chosen by trying several settings |
| Random loss weighting [@lin2022rlw] | Loss | Draws new task weights at random at every update |
| Uncertainty weighting [@kendall2018uncertainty] | Loss | Gives less weight to the task whose predictions are more uncertain |
| DWA [@liu2019mtan] | Loss | Gives more weight to the task whose loss is falling more slowly |
| GradNorm [@chen2018gradnorm] | Gradient | Adjusts the task weights so that both tasks learn at a similar speed |
| MGDA [@sener2018mgda] | Gradient | Combines the task gradients into the smallest update that improves both tasks |
| PCGrad [@yu2020pcgrad] | Gradient | When the task gradients conflict, removes the part of each that works against the other |
| GradDrop [@chen2020graddrop] | Gradient | Where the task gradients disagree in sign, keeps one sign chosen at random |
| IMTL [@liu2021imtl] | Loss and gradient | Scales the task gradients so that the update favors neither task, and keeps the losses at a similar size |
| GradVac [@wang2021gradvac] | Gradient | Adjusts the task gradients toward a target similarity tracked during training |
| CAGrad [@liu2021cagrad] | Gradient | Finds an update close to the average of the task gradients that most helps the task gaining least |
| Nash-MTL [@navon2022bargaining] | Gradient | Treats the tasks as players that bargain over the shared update |

: Multi-Task Optimizers {#tbl-optimizers tbl-colwidths="[24,14,62]"}

Studies disagree on whether SMTOs outperform fixed task weights. Five comparisons found little or no advantage. @vandenhende2022dense reported that fixed weights chosen by a grid search outperformed nearly all the automated methods, and both @xin2022mtohelp and @royer2023scalarization found that linear scalarization matched or outperformed the SMTOs. @xin2022mtohelp also found that tuning the training settings mattered more than the choice of optimizer. Similarly, equal weighting with regularization performed as well as the SMTOs in the comparison by @kurin2022unitary, and random weights performed comparably in that of @lin2022rlw, who proposed random weighting as a litmus test for new optimizers. In contrast, @gama2026uniform found that SMTOs outperformed equal weighting on more complex problems, although on two similar tasks they learned weights close to equal and matched it. These comparisons drew on images, robot tasks, molecules, translation, and multilingual text, and none involved disaster posts or Taglish. Because the optimizers act on the losses and gradients rather than on the text itself, they can be applied to posts in any language, as @xin2022mtohelp did across images and translation. How well they perform, however, depends on the problem [@gama2026uniform].

The optimizers also differ in training cost. Those that combine the gradients of the tasks must compute a separate gradient for each task, which requires additional time and memory, although this cost can be reduced by computing the gradients only at the output of the shared encoder [@lin2023libmtl]. In @xin2022mtohelp, computing a gradient for each task lowered training speed from about 12 to about 5 updates per second, and in @kurin2022unitary, the SMTOs took longer per epoch than equal weighting. @royer2023scalarization questioned whether removing conflicts at every step justifies the extra computation and memory. Such costs matter because they make deep learning research harder for those with fewer computing resources [@schwartz2020green]. Nevertheless, none of the multi-task disaster studies reviewed here reported training time or memory.

As @tbl-matrix shows, no earlier study combines Taglish posts, both tasks annotated on the same posts, several multi-task optimizers, and measured training cost.

## Synthesis of Related Literature and Studies

The reviewed studies point to three trends. First, datasets and models for disaster posts have been built mostly from English text, while the Philippine studies either trained a model for one task or relied on a commercial LLM [@lewis2025tapping; @ermino2022urgency; @somido2023actionable; @yute2021satellite; @caoile2025urdaneta]. Second, training classification together with a token-level task such as NER has produced mixed results [@zou2025typhoon; @khanal2021location; @ali2026humaidner], and one study traced negative transfer between the two to conflicting demands on the shared encoder [@zhu2025prefinetuning]. Third, studies disagree on whether SMTOs outperform fixed task weights, and their comparisons drew on images, robot tasks, molecules, translation, and multilingual text rather than disaster posts [@vandenhende2022dense; @xin2022mtohelp; @kurin2022unitary; @lin2022rlw; @royer2023scalarization; @gama2026uniform].

These trends leave two gaps. The first is the absence of a dataset in which the same Taglish posts are annotated for both humanitarian classification and NER. The only dataset identified with both kinds of annotation on the same posts is in English [@ali2026humaidner], and Taglish and Filipino have few annotated resources [@herrera2022tweettaglish; @cruz2022tagalog]. The first and second research questions address this gap. Accordingly, the study builds such a dataset, designs a multi-task model for it, and measures the performance of single-task models on it as the baseline.

The second gap is the absence of a comparison of multi-task optimizers for these two tasks on Taglish posts, in either negative transfer or training cost. None of the multi-task disaster studies compared more than two optimizers or reported training time or memory. Moreover, because the findings on multi-task optimizers depend on the problem [@gama2026uniform], results from other kinds of data cannot settle the choice for these posts. The third research question therefore compares the 13 optimizers in negative transfer, training time, and peak memory, and the fourth compares the final model, trained with the optimizer selected based on negative transfer, with the single-task models. Equal weighting serves as the reference in the third question, because several of the reviewed comparisons found that SMTOs did not outperform it.
